Superstructures and discrete choices¶

A superstructure represents the candidate units, streams and configurations considered in a design problem. Discrete variables select units or connections; continuous variables size and operate them. A structure omitted from this search space cannot be selected by optimization. Including an option does not guarantee its physical feasibility: balances, performance and specifications still have to be imposed.

BGW (1997), Example 15.2, pp. 500–502, considers three ammonia-process choices: tubular versus multibed-quench reactor, flash condensation versus absorption/distillation for product separation, and membrane versus no hydrogen recovery. Choosing exactly one option at each of three independent stages gives 23=82^3=823=8 combinations. A tree lists those combinations; a network superstructure shares units and can represent recycle and simultaneous routes. BGW’s network may represent combinations beyond the eight tree leaves if multiple paths are allowed. Exactly-one assumptions must therefore be written as constraints, rather than inferred from the drawing.

A general mixed-integer nonlinear program is

min⁡x,yf(x,y)s.t. h(x,y)=0,g(x,y)≤0,x∈X⊆Rn,y∈Y⊆Zt.\min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\quad\text{s.t. }\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{0},\quad \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\le\mathbf{0},\quad \mathbf{x}\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n,\quad \mathbf{y}\in Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^t.x,ymin​f(x,y)s.t. h(x,y)=0,g(x,y)≤0,x∈X⊆Rn,y∈Y⊆Zt.
(1)

Here x\mathbf{x}x is continuous and y\mathbf{y}y is integer. Binary variables restrict YYY to a subset of {0,1}t\{0,1\}^t{0,1}t. Both variable types can enter every function, including the equality constraints. In the linear special case the model is a MILP; if all its decision variables are integer it is an IP. An integer domain alone does not make nonlinear functions linear. Biegler (2010), Eq. (1.1), p. 3 and p. 4, gives the binary form and the class distinctions.

The reactor problem below is a compact superstructure with two parallel candidates. The two-reactor power-law NLP permits zero flows instead of explicit build switches; fixed charges will make selection a separate binary decision.

Optimizing across process alternatives¶

Reference: Example 15.3 from Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997). See handout

Assume that we have the choice of selecting two reactors (shown below) for the reaction A→BA \rightarrow BA→B. Reactor I has a higher conversion (80%) but it is more expensive; reactor II has a lower conversion (66.7%) but is cheaper. The cost of feed AAA is $5/kmol. Which process alternative (reactor I, reactor II, or both) has the minimum costs to make 10 kmol/hr of product B?

Let xrx_rxr​ be the feed flowrate into reactor rrr. Its cost contribution, including feed, is

Cr=ar(xr/xref)0.6+cfxr,xref=1 kmol/hr,cf=5 $/kmol.C_r=a_r(x_r/x_{\mathrm{ref}})^{0.6}+c_f x_r,\quad x_{\mathrm{ref}}=1~\mathrm{kmol/hr},\quad c_f=5~\mathrm{\$/kmol}.Cr​=ar​(xr​/xref​)0.6+cf​xr​,xref​=1 kmol/hr,cf​=5 $/kmol.
(2)

The reactor cost coefficients are rates in dollars per hour; the reference scale makes the power-law base dimensionless.

Count declared components before solving¶

With n=∣R∣n=|\mathcal R|n=∣R∣ reactors, the expanded model declares 1+2n1+2n1+2n continuous variables and n+2n+2n+2 linear equalities: one split, nnn conversions and one mixer. The original NLP has 1+2n1+2n1+2n lower-bounded variables and no upper bounds. Its objective is nonlinear even though its constraints are linear.

These equality rows are independent when every θr>0\theta_r>0θr​>0. In a linear combination of rows, the coefficient of x0x_0x0​ first forces the splitter multiplier to zero; the coefficient of each xrx_rxr​ then forces its conversion multiplier to zero, and the zrz_rzr​ coefficients force the mixer multiplier to zero. Thus the affine equality solution space has dimension (1+2n)−(n+2)=n−1(1+2n)-(n+2)=n-1(1+2n)−(n+2)=n−1. For P>0P>0P>0 it contains strictly positive reactor flows, so nonnegativity leaves a feasible set of that relative dimension. At its endpoints the bounds restrict the feasible directions. Counting rows alone would not establish rank or feasibility in a different model.

For two reactors this gives 5 variables, 4 independent equalities and one independent split choice.

The MILP below retains those 5 continuous variables and 4 equalities, and adds 2 binaries and 2 big-MMM inequalities. Its code also declares upper bounds of 20 on x0,x1,x2x_0,x_1,x_2x0​,x1​,x2​: 2 lower-only continuous variables and 5 variables bounded on both sides, including the binaries. The formulation without those explicit upper bounds has the same feasible set here: positive conversions and the production equality already imply x1≤12.5x_1\le12.5x1​≤12.5, x2≤15x_2\le15x2​≤15 and x0≤15x_0\le15x0​≤15. A declared bound is still counted even when redundant.

The NLP demonstration later replaces the two reactor-feed lower bounds by 10-6 to avoid singular derivatives. This slightly changes its feasible set; its output approximates the zero-flow endpoints.

Solve with the power-law cost model in Pyomo¶

The complete model uses the same sets, data and reference flow as the equations above.

Units in the power-law cost¶

The coefficients ar=5.5,4.0a_r=5.5,4.0ar​=5.5,4.0 are specified in dollars per hour when the numerical flow is measured in kmol/hr. With those coefficient units, arxr0.6a_r x_r^{0.6}ar​xr0.6​ does not have units of dollars per hour. A dimensional power is possible if its coefficient carries the corresponding compensating units; that is not how these coefficients are declared.

Write the implicit reference scale explicitly:

Cr=ar(xr/xref)0.6,xref=1 kmol/hr.C_r=a_r(x_r/x_{\mathrm{ref}})^{0.6},\qquad x_{\mathrm{ref}}=1~\mathrm{kmol/hr}.Cr​=ar​(xr​/xref​)0.6,xref​=1 kmol/hr.
(3)

Now the exponent acts on a dimensionless ratio and CrC_rCr​ has units of dollars per hour. The numerical objective is unchanged in the chosen units. If flow units change, convert xrefx_{\mathrm{ref}}xref​ too; changing only the numerical unit changes the fitted correlation. assert_units_consistent checks dimensional consistency, not physical adequacy, feasibility or optimality.

import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.environ import units as u
from pyomo.util.check_units import assert_units_consistent

# Pyomo's unit library has kmol and hr but no money, so declare a currency.
u.load_definitions_from_strings(["USD = [currency]"])

nlp = pyo.ConcreteModel()

## Define sets
nlp.REACTORS = pyo.Set(initialize=range(1, 3))

## Define parameters (data)

# Cost coefficient of reactor r, a_r [USD/hr]
cost_coefficient = {1: 5.5, 2: 4.0}
nlp.reactor_cost = pyo.Param(
    nlp.REACTORS, initialize=cost_coefficient, units=u.USD / u.hr
)

# Required product rate, P [kmol B/hr]
nlp.product_flowrate = pyo.Param(initialize=10.0, units=u.kmol / u.hr)

# Conversion of reactor r, theta_r [kmol B/kmol A]
reactor_conversion = {1: 0.8, 2: 2 / 3}
nlp.conversion = pyo.Param(nlp.REACTORS, initialize=reactor_conversion)

# Price of feed A, c_f [USD/kmol]
nlp.feed_cost = pyo.Param(initialize=5.0, units=u.USD / u.kmol)

# Reference flowrate for the economy-of-scale term, x_ref [kmol/hr]
nlp.flowrate_ref = pyo.Param(initialize=1.0, units=u.kmol / u.hr)


## Define variables

# Total feed of A, x_0 in the notes [kmol/hr]
nlp.feed_flowrate = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.kmol / u.hr)

# Feed into reactor r, x_r in the notes [kmol/hr]
nlp.reactor_feed = pyo.Var(
    nlp.REACTORS, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.kmol / u.hr
)

# Effluent leaving reactor r, z_r in the notes [kmol B/hr]
nlp.reactor_effluent = pyo.Var(
    nlp.REACTORS, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.kmol / u.hr
)

## Define constraints


# Add your solution here



## Define objective


# Total cost [USD/hr]. The exponent 0.6 is the economy-of-scale factor beta,
# applied to the flowrate scaled by x_ref so that the power is dimensionless.
@nlp.Objective()
def cost(b):
    return (
        sum(
            b.reactor_cost[r] * (b.reactor_feed[r] / b.flowrate_ref) ** (0.6)
            for r in b.REACTORS
        )
        + b.feed_cost * b.feed_flowrate
    )
# Inspect the model
nlp.pprint()

# Raises UnitsError if any constraint or the objective is dimensionally inconsistent
assert_units_consistent(nlp)

print("Units are consistent.")

Click to see the solution to the activity
# Mass balance over the splitter [kmol/hr]
@nlp.Constraint()
def inlet_split(b):
    return b.feed_flowrate == sum(b.reactor_feed[r] for r in b.REACTORS)


# Reactor conversion, z_r = theta_r * x_r [kmol B/hr]
@nlp.Constraint(nlp.REACTORS)
def reactor_performance(b, r):
    return b.reactor_effluent[r] == b.conversion[r] * b.reactor_feed[r]


# Mass balance over the mixer meets product requirements [kmol B/hr]
@nlp.Constraint()
def mixer(b):
    return b.product_flowrate == sum(b.reactor_effluent[r] for r in b.REACTORS)

Initialize to favor reactor I and solve¶

def initialize(model, reactor_choice=1):
    """Initialize all of the variables in the model to demonstrate local solutions

    Arguments:
        model: Pyomo model
        reactor_choice: 1 or 2

    Returns:
        nothing

    Action:
        initializes model

    """

    # Guess 20 kmol/hr feed of A
    model.feed_flowrate = 20.0

    # Either assign all of the feed to reactor 1 or 2
    if reactor_choice == 1:
        model.reactor_feed[1] = 20.0
        model.reactor_feed[2] = 0
    elif reactor_choice == 2:
        model.reactor_feed[1] = 0
        model.reactor_feed[2] = 20.0
    else:
        raise ValueError("Argument reactor_choice needs value 1 or 2.")

    # Based on the feed assignments, calculate effluent flowrate
    for r in model.REACTORS:
        model.reactor_effluent[r] = model.reactor_feed[r]() * model.conversion[r]


initialize(nlp, reactor_choice=1)
nlp.pprint()

Solve the current model and inspect its termination condition.

from pyomo.common.errors import ApplicationError

solver = pyo.SolverFactory("ipopt")
try:
    results = solver.solve(nlp, tee=True)
except ApplicationError as error:
    # This failure is intentional: the next cell explains the singular derivative.
    print(f"Expected solver failure: {type(error).__name__}: {error}")

What happened? 00.6 is fine --- it is 0. The derivative is not: ddxx0.6=0.6 x−0.4→∞\frac{d}{dx}x^{0.6} = 0.6\,x^{-0.4} \to \inftydxd​x0.6=0.6x−0.4→∞ as x→0x \to 0x→0, and Ipopt needs it. Read the message again: can't evaluate pow'(0,0.6) --- note the prime. Work around? Let’s set the lower bound to something really small:

small_number = 1e-6
for r in nlp.REACTORS:

    # Set lower bound
    nlp.reactor_feed[r].setlb(small_number)

    # Adjust initial point if needed
    nlp.reactor_feed[r] = max(nlp.reactor_feed[r](), small_number)

def print_solution(model):
    """Print variable names and values

    Arguments:
        model: Pyomo model

    print("\nObjective Name\t\tValue")
    for c in model.component_data_objects(pyo.Objective):
        print(c.name, "\t\t", pyo.value(c))

Interpret the two returned solutions using the complete cost profile below.

The reactor NLP has two local minima¶

Eliminating z1,z2,x0,x1z_1,z_2,x_0,x_1z1​,z2​,x0​,x1​ gives

x1(t)=10−(2/3)t0.8,0≤t=x2≤15,x_1(t)=\frac{10-(2/3)t}{0.8},\qquad 0\le t=x_2\le15,x1​(t)=0.810−(2/3)t​,0≤t=x2​≤15,
(4)
C(t)=5.5 x1(t)0.6+4t0.6+5[x1(t)+t],C(t)=5.5\,x_1(t)^{0.6}+4t^{0.6}+5[x_1(t)+t],C(t)=5.5x1​(t)0.6+4t0.6+5[x1​(t)+t],
(5)

where numerical flows use kmol/hr and the reference flow is 1 kmol/hr. On the open segment, each positive power-law term is strictly concave; the feed term is affine. Thus CCC is strictly concave and continuous on the closed segment. For 0≤λ≤10\le\lambda\le10≤λ≤1 and t=15λt=15\lambdat=15λ, concavity gives

C(t)≥(1−λ)C(0)+λC(15)≥min⁡{C(0),C(15)}.C(t)\ge(1-\lambda)C(0)+\lambda C(15)\ge\min\{C(0),C(15)\}.C(t)≥(1−λ)C(0)+λC(15)≥min{C(0),C(15)}.
(6)

Comparing endpoints therefore proves the global optimum of this particular model: reactor I only, x1=12.5,x2=0x_1=12.5,x_2=0x1​=12.5,x2​=0, costing about 87.53 dollars/hr. Reactor II alone costs about 95.31 dollars/hr. The interior maximum is at x2≈11.26x_2\approx11.26x2​≈11.26; BGW’s sketch labels it 11.4. These values use the exact conversion 2/32/32/3, rather than the rounded 0.67 in the printed equations.

Concavity alone does not make both endpoints local minima. Here the incoming unused-reactor cost has a positive h0.6h^{0.6}h0.6 term that dominates the O(h)O(h)O(h) change in the active reactor and feed. Near t=0t=0t=0, C(t)−C(0)=4t0.6+O(t)>0C(t)-C(0)=4t^{0.6}+O(t)>0C(t)−C(0)=4t0.6+O(t)>0; near t=15t=15t=15, C(15−h)−C(15)=5.5(5h/6)0.6+O(h)>0C(15-h)-C(15)=5.5(5h/6)^{0.6}+O(h)>0C(15−h)−C(15)=5.5(5h/6)0.6+O(h)>0. Hence both endpoints are strict local minima relative to the feasible segment.

The derivative of x0.6x^{0.6}x0.6 is singular at zero. The usual differentiable KKT theorem cannot be applied at these exact endpoints. The notebook instead solves the slightly perturbed model with reactor-feed lower bounds 10-6. Its two initializations demonstrate two local returns; there is no general rule that a local solver selects the nearest endpoint, and an optimal termination message alone does not prove the global result. The endpoint comparison above supplies that proof.

The analytic curve is owned by figures/plots/reactor-concave-local-minima.py; it is not a second implementation of solver output. Source: BGW (1997), Example 15.3, pp. 509–511.

Linearized Discrete Cost Model¶

Replace the power-law equipment cost by a fixed charge plus a constant marginal cost. This gives a different cost approximation whose resulting model is a MILP. A globally solved MILP certifies that approximation; it does not certify an arbitrary original nonlinear cost model. The on/off link below imposes an upper capacity when a reactor is selected. It does not impose a positive minimum operating flow.

Fixed charges and what the binary means¶

For each reactor introduce yr∈{0,1}y_r\in\{0,1\}yr​∈{0,1} and impose 0≤xr≤Mryr0\le x_r\le M_r y_r0≤xr​≤Mr​yr​. Its equipment cost is bˉryr+aˉrxr\bar b_r y_r+\bar a_r x_rbˉr​yr​+aˉr​xr​, with (bˉ1,bˉ2)=(7.5,5.5)(\bar b_1,\bar b_2)=(7.5,5.5)(bˉ1​,bˉ2​)=(7.5,5.5) dollars/hr and (aˉ1,aˉ2)=(1.4,1.0)(\bar a_1,\bar a_2)=(1.4,1.0)(aˉ1​,aˉ2​)=(1.4,1.0) dollars/kmol. Add the feed cost 5x05x_05x0​. A one-time capital expense must be annualized or otherwise put on the same time basis before combining it with a rate in dollars/hr.

The link proves yr=0⇒xr=0y_r=0\Rightarrow x_r=0yr​=0⇒xr​=0, or equivalently xr>0⇒yr=1x_r>0\Rightarrow y_r=1xr​>0⇒yr​=1. It permits yr=1,xr=0y_r=1,x_r=0yr​=1,xr​=0: a selected unit can be idle. With a positive fixed charge and no other reason to retain an idle unit, minimization switches it off. A positive minimum throughput would require the additional row Lryr≤xrL_r y_r\le x_rLr​yr​≤xr​ for a justified Lr>0L_r>0Lr​>0.

After minimizing over a free switch for one unit, its cost as a function of flow is piecewise:

C^r(xr)={0,xr=0,bˉr+aˉrxr,0<xr≤Mr.\widehat C_r(x_r)=\begin{cases}0,&x_r=0,\\\bar b_r+\bar a_r x_r,&0<x_r\le M_r.\end{cases}Cr​(xr​)={0,bˉr​+aˉr​xr​,​xr​=0,0<xr​≤Mr​.​
(7)

This is a discontinuous function of xrx_rxr​ alone. The binary gives it a linear mixed-integer representation; it is not correct to say no such scalar function exists. The plotted zero-cost point represents an unbuilt unit, and the positive-flow branch represents a selected unit.

The shared analytic figure contains equipment-only and equipment-plus-feed panels and an origin inset. The separate exploratory cell below lets you change the two total-cost lines. It plots the selected-unit branch at zero as well; the shared figure distinguishes that branch from the unbuilt zero-cost point. Both implementations serve these stated, different roles.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

feed = np.linspace(0, 20, 101)

# Price of feed A, c_f [USD/kmol] -- the same for both reactors
c_feed = 5

for reactor in [1, 2]:

    if reactor == 1:
        c = 5.5
        c_linear = 6.4
        c_fixed = 7.5
        color = "r"
    elif reactor == 2:
        c = 4.0
        c_linear = 6.0
        c_fixed = 5.5
        color = "b"
    else:
        break

    cost_continuous = c * (feed) ** (0.6) + c_feed * feed
    cost_linearized = c_linear * feed + c_fixed

    plt.plot(
        feed,
        cost_continuous,
        label="Reactor " + str(reactor) + " (continuous)",
        color=color,
        linestyle="-",
    )
    plt.plot(
        feed,
        cost_linearized,
        label="Reactor " + str(reactor) + " (linearized)",
        color=color,
        linestyle="--",
    )

plt.legend()
plt.xlabel("Feed Flowrate (kmol/hr)")
plt.ylabel(r"Cost (\$/hr)")
plt.show()

Define binary variable:

yr={1if reactor r is selected0otherwise y_r = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if reactor } r \text{ is selected} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}yr​={10​if reactor r is selectedotherwise​

Add logical constraints to include the valid upper bound (20 kmol/hr):

xr≤20yr,∀r∈R x_r \leq 20 y_r, \quad \forall r \in \mathcal{R}xr​≤20yr​,∀r∈R

Thus if yr=0y_r = 0yr​=0, then xr=0x_r = 0xr​=0

Finally, we can define the new linearized reactor cost model:

Reactor I:7.5y1+1.4x1Reactor II:5.5y2+1.0x2\begin{align*} \text{Reactor I:} \quad & 7.5 y_1 + 1.4 x_1 \\ \text{Reactor II:} \quad & 5.5 y_2 + 1.0 x_2 \end{align*}Reactor I:Reactor II:​7.5y1​+1.4x1​5.5y2​+1.0x2​​
(8)

Recall that x0=x1+x2x_0 = x_1 + x_2x0​=x1​+x2​. Thus, the feed cost is 5x0=5x1+5x25x_0 = 5 x_1 + 5 x_25x0​=5x1​+5x2​.

Putting this all together gives the following MILP optimization problem:

min⁡x,yC=7.5y1+6.4x1+5.5y2+6.0x2s.t.0.8x1+(2/3)x2=10x1−20y1≤0x2−20y2≤0x1,x2≥0,y1,y2∈{0,1}\begin{align*} \min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \quad & C = 7.5 y_1 + 6.4 x_1 + 5.5 y_2 + 6.0 x_2 \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & 0.8 x_1 + (2/3) x_2 = 10 \\ & x_1 - 20 y_1 \leq 0 \\ & x_2 - 20 y_2 \leq 0 \\ & x_1, x_2 \geq 0, \quad y_1, y_2 \in \{0, 1\} \end{align*}x,ymin​s.t.​C=7.5y1​+6.4x1​+5.5y2​+6.0x2​0.8x1​+(2/3)x2​=10x1​−20y1​≤0x2​−20y2​≤0x1​,x2​≥0,y1​,y2​∈{0,1}​
(9)

Enumerate the four binary assignments¶

For each fixed (y1,y2)(y_1,y_2)(y1​,y2​), solve the remaining LP. The same production target, conversions and costs apply in every row.

y1y_1y1​y2y_2y2​x1x_1x1​x2x_2x2​Cost ($/hr)Interpretation
0000infeasible0.8x1+(2/3)x2=0≠100.8x_1+(2/3)x_2=0\ne100.8x1​+(2/3)x2​=0=10
1012.5087.5reactor I alone
0101595.5reactor II alone
1112.5093.0reactor II is selected but idle and still costs 5.5

The marginal costs per unit of product, including feed, are 6.4/0.8=86.4/0.8=86.4/0.8=8 for reactor I and 6/(2/3)=96/(2/3)=96/(2/3)=9 for reactor II. Thus, when both are selected, all production still uses I. The cheapest feasible row proves the global optimum of this two-reactor MILP. Its agreement in reactor choice with the nonlinear model is specific to these data; their objective values differ.

With ttt binary choices, exhaustive enumeration has 2t2^t2t assignments: 1,024 at t=10t=10t=10 and 1,073,741,824 at t=30t=30t=30. General integer variables need their own finite bounds before exhaustive enumeration is finite. Practical methods discard groups using valid bounds rather than solving every assignment. The complete branch-and-bound algorithm is taught in the course’s MINLP Algorithms guide; this section supplies the modeling example. Source: BGW (1997), pp. 512–513.

Solve with Pyomo¶

Create and inspect the model. The explicit upper bounds on feed variables are redundant for these data, but remain part of its declared component count.

milp = pyo.ConcreteModel()

## Define sets
milp.REACTORS = pyo.Set(initialize=range(1, 3))

## Define parameters (data)

# Big-M throughput limit, M [kmol/hr]
milp.max_flowrate = pyo.Param(initialize=20.0, units=u.kmol / u.hr)

# Marginal (linear) cost of reactor r, abar_r [USD/kmol]
cost_coefficient1 = {1: 1.4, 2: 1.0}
milp.reactor_cost_linear = pyo.Param(
    milp.REACTORS, initialize=cost_coefficient1, units=u.USD / u.kmol
)

# Fixed charge for selecting reactor r, bbar_r [USD/hr]
cost_coefficient2 = {1: 7.5, 2: 5.5}
milp.reactor_cost_fixed = pyo.Param(
    milp.REACTORS, initialize=cost_coefficient2, units=u.USD / u.hr
)

# Required product rate, P [kmol B/hr]
milp.product_flowrate = pyo.Param(initialize=10.0, units=u.kmol / u.hr)

# Conversion of reactor r, theta_r [kmol B/kmol A]
reactor_conversion = {1: 0.8, 2: 2 / 3}
milp.conversion = pyo.Param(milp.REACTORS, initialize=reactor_conversion)

# Price of feed A, c_f [USD/kmol]
milp.feed_cost = pyo.Param(initialize=5.0, units=u.USD / u.kmol)


## Define variables

# Total feed of A, x_0 in the notes [kmol/hr]
milp.feed_flowrate = pyo.Var(
    domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, bounds=(0, milp.max_flowrate), units=u.kmol / u.hr
)

# Feed into reactor r, x_r in the notes [kmol/hr]
milp.reactor_feed = pyo.Var(
    milp.REACTORS,
    domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals,
    bounds=(0, milp.max_flowrate),
    units=u.kmol / u.hr,
)

# Effluent leaving reactor r, z_r in the notes [kmol B/hr]
milp.reactor_effluent = pyo.Var(
    milp.REACTORS, domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals, units=u.kmol / u.hr
)

# Binary variables: y_r = 1 if reactor r is selected
# Add your solution here

## Define constraints


# Mass balance over the splitter [kmol/hr]
@milp.Constraint()
def inlet_split(b):
    return b.feed_flowrate == sum(b.reactor_feed[r] for r in b.REACTORS)


# Reactor conversion, z_r = theta_r * x_r [kmol B/hr]
@milp.Constraint(milp.REACTORS)
def reactor_performance(b, r):
    return b.reactor_effluent[r] == b.conversion[r] * b.reactor_feed[r]


# Mass balance over the mixer meets product requirements [kmol B/hr]
@milp.Constraint()
def mixer(b):
    return b.product_flowrate == sum(b.reactor_effluent[r] for r in b.REACTORS)



# On/off link x_r <= M y_r [kmol/hr].
# Add your solution here

# Equipment and feed cost [USD/hr].
# Add your solution here

# Inspect the model
milp.pprint()

# Raises UnitsError if any constraint or the objective is dimensionally inconsistent
assert_units_consistent(milp)

print("Units are consistent.")

# Binary variables: y_r = 1 if reactor r is selected
milp.reactor_boolean = pyo.Var(milp.REACTORS, domain=pyo.Binary)


# Big-M logical constraint, x_r <= M * y_r [kmol/hr]
@milp.Constraint(milp.REACTORS)
def toggle_reactor(b, r):
    return b.reactor_feed[r] <= b.reactor_boolean[r] * b.max_flowrate


# Total cost [USD/hr]
@milp.Objective()
def cost(b):
    return (
        sum(
            b.reactor_cost_linear[r] * b.reactor_feed[r]
            + b.reactor_cost_fixed[r] * b.reactor_boolean[r]
            for r in b.REACTORS
        )
        + b.feed_cost * b.feed_flowrate
    )

Solve the model using appsi_highs (the course default for LPs and MILPs), bonmin, gurobi (need license), or cplex (need license).

Valid bounds and the LP relaxation¶

For a nonnegative flow, xr≤Mryrx_r\le M_r y_rxr​≤Mr​yr​ is valid only when MrM_rMr​ is at least the largest feasible value of xrx_rxr​ in the intended physical model. With θr>0\theta_r>0θr​>0, x≥0x\ge0x≥0 and ∑rθrxr=P\sum_r\theta_r x_r=P∑r​θr​xr​=P, every term is at most PPP, so

xr≤P/θr;M1=12.5,M2=15x_r\le P/\theta_r;\qquad M_1=12.5,\quad M_2=15xr​≤P/θr​;M1​=12.5,M2​=15
(10)

are valid individual bounds here. The common value 20 is valid but weaker. A bound of 10 excludes the feasible reactor-I-only design. Bounds must be re-derived if conversion, production requirements, additional reactions or flow signs change.

Relaxing a binary switch gives 0≤yr≤10\le y_r\le10≤yr​≤1. At x1=12.5x_1=12.5x1​=12.5, the link requires y1≥12.5/M1y_1\ge12.5/M_1y1​≥12.5/M1​. With common M=20M=20M=20, the smallest switch is 0.625; with 20,000 it is 0.000625. The physical production equality already bounds both flows, so increasing this valid logical bound does not add new integer designs in this particular example. It does allow the LP to pay a smaller fraction of the fixed charge. The scalar switch picture below omits the reactor production equality and explicit physical caps so its mechanism is visible.

For fixed MrM_rMr​, the single-unit set {(0,0)}∪{(x,1):0≤x≤Mr}\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,1):0\le x\le M_r\}{(0,0)}∪{(x,1):0≤x≤Mr​} has convex hull 0≤y≤10\le y\le10≤y≤1, 0≤x≤Mry0\le x\le M_r y0≤x≤Mr​y. If y>0y>0y>0, any relaxed point equals (1−y)(0,0)+y(x/y,1)(1-y)(0,0)+y(x/y,1)(1−y)(0,0)+y(x/y,1); the y=0y=0y=0 case is (0,0)(0,0)(0,0). This proof concerns one switch. Intersecting many such hulls with balances does not generally give the convex hull of the whole process.

For minimization the relaxed feasible set contains every integer-feasible point, so its globally optimal value is a lower bound on the MILP optimum, provided the same objective is used. The table computed below solves the complete reactor model, not just the scalar picture. The common bound of 20 gives 84.6875 dollars/hr; 20,000 gives 80.0046875; the individual production bounds give 87.5 and close the objective gap for these data. This is not a general integrality guarantee.

Source: BGW (1997), Eqs. (15.10)–(15.12), p. 512, and Appendix A, §A.3.2, pp. 758, 760–761. The production-bound and convex-combination arguments are supplied here in full.

# Count declared rows and bounds, rather than subtracting rows from variables.
def declared_counts(model):
    variables = list(model.component_data_objects(pyo.Var))
    rows = list(model.component_data_objects(pyo.Constraint, active=True))
    return dict(
        continuous=sum(v.is_continuous() for v in variables),
        binary=sum(v.is_binary() for v in variables),
        linear_equalities=sum(c.equality and c.body.polynomial_degree() in (0, 1) for c in rows),
        linear_inequalities=sum(not c.equality and c.body.polynomial_degree() in (0, 1) for c in rows),
        lower_only=sum(v.lb is not None and v.ub is None for v in variables),
        both_bounds=sum(v.lb is not None and v.ub is not None for v in variables),
    )

print("NLP declarations:", declared_counts(nlp))
print("MILP declarations:", declared_counts(milp))
highs = pyo.SolverFactory("appsi_highs")
print("Fixed binaries | x1 | x2 | cost [USD/hr]")
for first, second in [(0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)]:
    fixed = milp.clone()
    fixed.reactor_boolean[1].fix(first)
    fixed.reactor_boolean[2].fix(second)
    result = highs.solve(fixed, load_solutions=False)
    if result.solver.termination_condition == pyo.TerminationCondition.infeasible:
        print(f"{first}{second}: infeasible")
    else:
        assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(result)
        fixed.solutions.load_from(result)
        print(f"{first}{second}: {pyo.value(fixed.reactor_feed[1]):.4f} | "
              f"{pyo.value(fixed.reactor_feed[2]):.4f} | {pyo.value(fixed.cost):.4f}")

print("LP bound | y1 | x1 | cost [USD/hr]")
for label, bound in [("M=20", 20.0), ("M=20000", 20000.0), ("production bounds", None)]:
    relaxed = milp.clone()
    pyo.TransformationFactory("core.relax_integer_vars").apply_to(relaxed)
    if bound is not None:
        relaxed.max_flowrate.set_value(bound)
    else:
        for r in relaxed.REACTORS:
            capacity = relaxed.product_flowrate / relaxed.conversion[r]
            relaxed.toggle_reactor[r].set_value(
                relaxed.reactor_feed[r] <= capacity * relaxed.reactor_boolean[r])
    result = highs.solve(relaxed)
    assert pyo.check_optimal_termination(result)
    print(f"{label}: {pyo.value(relaxed.reactor_boolean[1]):.8f} | "
          f"{pyo.value(relaxed.reactor_feed[1]):.4f} | {pyo.value(relaxed.cost):.7f}")

m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

# Declare variables with bounds
m.x1 = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)
m.x2 = pyo.Var(domain=pyo.NonNegativeReals)

# Constraint 3
m.con3 = pyo.Constraint(expr=-m.x1 + m.x2 >= 5)

# Objective
m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=m.x2)

# Print model
m.pprint()

Why rounding does not always work¶

Special forms and modeling applications¶

A common special MINLP form is

min⁡x,ycTy+f(x)s.t. h(x)=0,g(x)+Ay≤0,x∈X,y∈{0,1}t.\min_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{y}+f(\mathbf{x})\quad\text{s.t. }\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0},\quad \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}\le\mathbf{0},\quad \mathbf{x}\in X,\quad \mathbf{y}\in\{0,1\}^t.x,ymin​cTy+f(x)s.t. h(x)=0,g(x)+Ay≤0,x∈X,y∈{0,1}t.
(13)

Here fixed charges are linear in y\mathbf{y}y and binaries enter the coupling inequalities linearly. The matrix A\mathbf{A}A contains signed coefficients; it is not the positive scalar upper bound MMM. This is BGW problem (P1), p. 513, a specialization of the general form above. Binaries can enter nonlinear equalities in the general form, so h(x)\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})h(x) is not a restriction to impose on all MINLPs.

OperationResult
Fix all binaries to a specified assignmentcontinuous NLP subproblem; it can be infeasible
Relax binaries to their bounds 0≤y≤10\le\mathbf{y}\le10≤y≤1continuous NLP relaxation
Use affine objective and constraint expressions, retaining binariesMILP
Start with a MILP and fix or relax every integer variableLP subproblem or LP relaxation

Replacing a nonlinear cost by an affine approximation changes the model; it is not an exact identity. For a general nonlinear relaxation, a local returned objective need not be a lower bound: the lower-bound statement requires the globally minimized relaxation.

Scheduling and planning use binaries for assignments, operating campaigns and facility locations. Unit commitment uses start/on decisions with continuous output; nonlinear heat-rate functions lead to MINLP, while suitable linear data/formulations lead to MILP. Discrete equipment design can select tray numbers, feed-tray location, exchanger connections or catalog sizes. Biegler (2010), Table 1.1, p. 6 and Exercise 6, p. 16, gives engineering examples. Further worked MO-book models: workforce shift scheduling, machine scheduling, facility location, dinner seating, and exam-room scheduling.

Ljyj≤γj≤Ujyj.L_j y_j\le\gamma_j\le U_j y_j.Lj​yj​≤γj​≤Uj​yj​.
(14)

Both sides matter: yj=0y_j=0yj​=0 then forces γj=0\gamma_j=0γj​=0. The nonnegative reactor’s one-sided switch does not apply unchanged to a coefficient that can be negative. A cardinality budget ∑jyj≤k\sum_jy_j\le k∑j​yj​≤k limits selected terms. The bound validity and choice of kkk are additional modeling decisions.

Some nonsmooth functions have continuous reformulations: positive absolute-value penalties and max epigraphs can be LPs, as developed in the continuous formulation reference. Exact nonconvex graph relations or logical alternatives may require binaries. It is incorrect to claim that every absolute value or maximum introduces integer variables.

Broader modeling and theory references: H. P. Williams, Model Building in Mathematical Programming, 5th ed., Wiley, 2013; G. L. Nemhauser and L. A. Wolsey, Integer and Combinatorial Optimization, Wiley, 1988.

The restriction excludes unused binary codes when the range size is not a power of two. The case U=LU=LU=L needs no binary. This represents a bounded integer domain; it does not linearize a nonlinear function of that integer.

Further literature on superstructure optimization¶

The lecture introduces the representation and a two-unit model. The extended reading list is retained here for independent study: reviews and frameworks first, then carbon capture/utilization, membrane separation, water and exchanger networks, energy systems, intensification and waste systems. These are the existing course references; the short lecture does not teach each application.

  • Naonori Nishida et al. (1981), A Review of Process Synthesis.

  • Qi Chen et al. (2017), Recent Developments and Challenges in Optimization-Based Process Synthesis.

  • Luca Mencarelli et al. (2020), A Review on Superstructure Optimization Approaches in Process System Engineering.

  • Efstratios N. Pistikopoulos et al. (2024), Advanced Modeling and Optimization Strategies for Process Synthesis.

  • J. Rafael Alcántara-Avila (2023), 50 Years of Optimization in Japan Using Superstructures.

  • Hector Yeomans et al. (1999), A Systematic Modeling Framework of Superstructure Optimization in Process Synthesis.

  • Zev Friedman et al. (2013), Block-Oriented Modeling of Superstructure Optimization Problems.

  • Sunwoo Kim et al. (2026), Decarbonization as a Systems and Control Challenge: From Superstructure Optimization to Multi-Period Decision-Making under Uncertainty.

  • Xuechong Ding et al. (2024), Superstructure-Based Carbon Capture and Utilization Process Design.

  • Natsayi Chiwaye et al. (2025), Superstructure-Based Optimization of Membrane Gas Separation Processes: A Review.

  • Rouzbeh Ramezani et al. (2023), Using a Superstructure Approach for Techno-Economic Analysis of Membrane Processes.

  • Ignacio E. Grossmann et al. (2014), Review of Optimization Models for Integrated Process Water Networks and Their Application to Biofuel Processes.

  • Elvis Ahmetović et al. (2011), Global Superstructure Optimization for the Design of Integrated Process Water Networks.

  • Ramkumar Karuppiah et al. (2006), Global Optimization for the Synthesis of Integrated Water Systems in Chemical Processes.

  • Siqi Liu et al. (2026), Advancements in Superstructures Design and Solver Approaches for Heat and Mass Exchange Network Synthesis.

  • Jian Gong et al. (2015), Sustainable Design and Synthesis of Energy Systems.

  • Philip Voll et al. (2013), Automated Superstructure-Based Synthesis and Optimization of Distributed Energy Supply Systems.

  • Mirko Skiborowski (2018), Process Synthesis and Design Methods for Process Intensification.

  • Channarong Puchongkawarin et al. (2020), Development of a Superstructure Optimization Framework for the Design of Municipal Solid Waste Facilities.
